lede: Most work on a table is a small change to its columns: one more value worked out, one renamed for a report, one removed before it's shared. `withColumn`, `withColumnRenamed` and `drop` do exactly that and leave everything else in place.
objectives: Add a new column, or replace one, with `withColumn`
Put the same value on every row with `F.lit`
Remove columns with `drop`, and know which mistakes Spark doesn't warn you about

blocks.md:
The `employees` table above has one row per person at a small company. On this page it's loaded as a DataFrame called `employees`, and `F` is `pyspark.sql.functions`.

`select` (lesson 9) gives back only the columns you list. When you want to keep **all** the columns and change just one, listing all fourteen gets old fast. `df.withColumn("name", column)` keeps every column and adds one more at the end, worked out for each row.

blocks.title: Add a column
blocks.code:
from pyspark.sql import functions as F

raised = employees.withColumn("new_salary", F.col("salary") + 2500)
raised.select("employee_id", "salary", "new_salary").show(4)
print(len(employees.columns), "columns before,", len(raised.columns), "after")
blocks.note: `withColumn` returned all fourteen columns plus `new_salary`; `select` only trims what's printed. `employees` itself still has fourteen.

blocks.md:
If the name is one the table already has, `withColumn` **replaces** that column instead, and it stays in the same position.

The second argument must be a column, not a plain Python value. For the same value on every row, wrap it in `F.lit(...)`. `withColumns` takes a dict of names and columns and adds several in one step.

blocks.title: Replace a column and add fixed values
blocks.code:
from pyspark.sql import functions as F

next_year = employees.withColumn("level", F.col("level") + 1)
next_year.select("employee_id", "job_title", "level").show(3)

tagged = employees.withColumns({"currency": F.lit("USD"), "review_year": F.lit(2026)})
tagged.select("employee_id", "salary", "currency", "review_year").show(3)
tagged.printSchema()
blocks.note: `level` is changed where it was, not added again. `F.lit("USD")` is a text column and `F.lit(2026)` a whole number, the same on every row.

blocks.title: A plain value instead of a column
blocks.note: `withColumn` needs a column as its second argument. Write `F.lit(5000)` for a fixed value.

blocks.md:
`withColumnRenamed("old", "new")` renames one column and keeps it where it was; `withColumnsRenamed` takes a dict to rename several. `drop("a", "b")` removes columns.

Both are forgiving in a way that can hide a typo: **renaming or dropping a column that doesn't exist does nothing**, with no error. Check `columns` when it matters.

blocks.title: Rename and drop
blocks.note: The renamed columns keep their places. The three dropped columns are gone and the rest keep their order.

blocks.title: A typo that Spark lets through
blocks.note: There's no `dept_id` and no `phone_number` in `employees`, so nothing was renamed or dropped and nothing complained. The columns are exactly as before.

concept.prompt: `employees` already has a `level` column. What does `employees.withColumn("level", F.col("level") + 1)` give back?
choices: A second `level` column at the end
The same columns, with `level` replaced in its usual position
concept.why: When the name already exists, `withColumn` replaces that column and keeps its position. A new name is added at the end.

concept.prompt: Which line adds a column with the text `USD` on every row?
concept.why: `F.lit` turns a plain value into a column. A bare `"USD"` is refused, and `F.col("USD")` looks for a column named USD.

concept.prompt: What happens with `employees.drop("phone_number")` when there's no column with that name?
choices: It stops with an error naming the missing column
It drops the column that is closest in name, `phone`
Nothing: the DataFrame comes back unchanged
concept.why: `drop` and `withColumnRenamed` quietly ignore names that aren't there, so a typo doesn't raise an error. Check `columns` if you're not sure.

review: `withColumn("name", column)` keeps every column and adds one at the end, or replaces it in place if the name exists.
`withColumns({...})` adds or replaces several columns at once.
The second argument must be a column. Use `F.lit(value)` for the same value on every row.
`withColumnRenamed("old", "new")` and `withColumnsRenamed({...})` rename and keep the position.
`drop("a", "b")` removes columns. Renaming or dropping a name that isn't there does nothing, with no error.
